faqs.q: How is bat exclusion priced for a Hollins home with a tall, older roofline?
faqs.a: Roofline complexity is the price driver. A two-story Hollins home with dormers, a brick chimney, and multiple roof planes can have a dozen gaps a bat colony uses, and each one must be found, fitted or sealed, and checked — plus guano cleanup scaled to how long the colony has been resident. We inspect from ladder and attic both, quote the full exclusion and cleanup in writing, and schedule the exit-fitting outside the maternity season our permit conditions set, May 1 through August 15.

faqs.q: Why do squirrels keep getting into Hollins attics even after repairs?
faqs.a: Usually because the repair covered the hole the squirrels were seen using, not the canopy highway that delivered them. In Hollins, oaks overhang roofs on most streets, and a gray squirrel that loses one soffit entry simply tests the gable vent, the chimney flashing, and the addition joint until something gives. Lasting work means sealing the full roofline in material squirrels cannot chew and cutting limbs back so the roof is no longer a branch landing — do both, and Hollins attics tend to stay quiet.

Hollins.wildlife_intro:
North of Roanoke, Hollins is a creek valley with a university in it. Tinker Creek and the wooded Carvins Cove watershed wrap the neighborhood in green, and Hollins University's historic brick buildings and faculty homes sit under some of the oldest canopy in the county. Big brown bats are the Hollins signature — summer colonies in the tall attics of campus-era houses and halls — followed by gray squirrels working the oak canopy straight onto ranch and split-level roofs, and raccoons in the brick chimneys along the creek.

Shaded lots change the maintenance math here: limbs stay over roofs, gutters stay full, and small soffit gaps go unnoticed for years behind the leaves. Our Hollins work pairs the animal job with the tree-and-roofline conversation — which limbs to cut back, which vents to screen — because in this valley the next entry point is usually already growing toward the house.

faqs.q: How do you quote groundhog removal for a Catawba farm with several burrow systems?
faqs.a: We walk the systems with you and rank them by what they threaten. A burrow undermining a barn slab or a silo pad is structural work and goes first; a system in a distant field bank may honestly be one to monitor. Each system is quoted on its own — entrances, access for equipment, and the backfilling and fencing advice that follows — so the price tracks the farm's real priorities instead of a per-animal guess. Groundhogs are a designated nuisance species in Virginia, so the permit side is simple; the planning is the service.

faqs.q: Are the rattlesnakes above Catawba something I need to worry about at my house?
faqs.a: Mostly, they are something to respect at a distance. Timber rattlesnakes den and bask on the rocky, sunlit ridges above the valley — McAfee Knob country — and rarely come down to houses; Catawba's valley-floor snake calls are far more often black rat snakes or copperheads near rock walls and woodpiles. Never approach any snake you cannot identify. If a rattlesnake takes up residence where it truly cannot be avoided, a permit holder can move a non-listed snake a short distance to suitable habitat in the same or a neighboring county, with the release-site landowner's written permission, reported to the Virginia Department of Wildlife Resources — and that is the most anyone should promise.

Catawba.wildlife_intro:
Catawba is the farm valley underneath McAfee Knob — the Appalachian Trail's most photographed overlook draws the hikers, but the valley floor is hay fields, cattle, and farmhouses along Catawba Creek, with forested ridge on both sides. Groundhogs own this call sheet: they burrow the field edges, undermine barn and silo slabs, and dig under farmhouse porches within sight of the pastures they feed in. Raccoons work the corn and the feed rooms, and the ridges send down snakes — black rat snakes in the barns, copperheads in the rock and brush, and timber rattlesnakes on the high rocky slopes, where they are left strictly alone.

Valley work in Catawba is farm work. We time groundhog jobs around hay and livestock, treat the burrow systems threatening concrete and stock first, and give the snake calls the identification-first respect mountain country requires — including knowing that a spotted skunk, a declining species found only in Virginia's west, is a leave-alone call to DWR, not a trapping job.

faqs.q: What does a proper mole program for a Glenvar lawn actually include?
faqs.a: It includes mapping before trapping. Moles are solitary and territorial, so a Glenvar yard usually holds a few animals working defined travel runs between feeding areas — we probe and flag the active runs, set traps in those runs, and check them daily as Virginia law requires. Pricing follows the yard's size and the number of active systems, quoted after the mapping walk. We also tell you straight that new moles recolonize good river-bottom soil, so most Glenvar lawns are quoted as a season program with follow-up visits priced in, not a single afternoon.

faqs.q: Geese have claimed the pond by our Glenvar homes — what can actually be done?
faqs.a: Canada geese are federally protected, so removal is not a service anyone can sell you. What works on subdivision ponds and fields is persistence: a taller planted edge at the waterline, which geese avoid because it hides predators, consistent hazing when flocks first settle, and a strict no-feeding norm in the neighborhood. Egg and nest work exists only under a federal depredation framework that starts with registering with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service. We can assess your pond and lay out the deterrence sequence — but the crew that promises to simply take the geese away is promising something unlawful.

Glenvar.wildlife_intro:
Glenvar's suburbs spread along the Roanoke River toward Salem, and flat, well-watered river ground makes this mole country first and foremost. Eastern moles ridge the big lawns and the school athletic fields after every wet spell, following the earthworms the bottomland soil grows so well — most Glenvar calls start with a yard that looks plowed by morning. The river adds its own traffic: raccoons den in the older ranch attics along the corridor, and Canada geese graze the open fields and pond edges, protected birds that call for deterrence rather than removal.

A Glenvar season has a rhythm we plan around: mole trapping in the active spring and fall runs, raccoon families out of attics before the young are mobile, and goose hazing set up before nesting starts. What we will not do is sell a Glenvar homeowner a one-visit miracle for any of the three — river ground keeps producing all of them, and the honest service is a mapped, maintained program rather than a promise.
